summary: Defines GS2, a family of SASL mechanisms that lets any suitable GSS-API mechanism be used for authentication in SASL. It improves on the older SASL GSSAPI mechanism, can use fewer messages, and supports negotiable channel binding. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: GS2 lets a connection-based application use a Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) mechanism through the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL). It adds a compact header and can bind authentication to a secure channel, but it does not encrypt or protect later application data by itself.

questions: what does the plus suffix mean in sasl mechanism names
subtitle: Connects GSS-API authentication mechanisms to SASL with negotiable channel binding.

tldr.problem: The earlier SASL bridge for GSS-API mechanisms was less general, could use more exchange messages, and did not support channel binding.
tldr.mechanism: GS2 wraps GSS-API context tokens for SASL and adds a small header to identify authorization identity and negotiate whether to bind authentication to an external secure channel.
tldr.outcome: Applications can use suitable GSS-API mechanisms through SASL, but GS2 does not provide its own data-protection layer. RFC 5801 is updated by RFC 9266.

today: RFC 5801 is a Proposed Standard for the GS2 SASL mechanism family and is updated by RFC 9266.

sections.title: Bridging GSS-API and SASL
sections.content:
GSS-API is a framework for security mechanisms, while SASL is a framework for authentication and security layers in connection-based protocols. GS2 defines how a GSS-API mechanism can act as a SASL mechanism.

Compared with the older bridge, GS2 is more general, may need fewer messages for authentication, and supports channel binding. It only supports GSS-API mechanisms that provide channel binding and mutual authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: GS2 allows an application that speaks SASL to use an eligible GSS-API authentication mechanism. It improves the older bridge by supporting channel binding and, in some cases, fewer messages.

sections.title: Names for Mechanisms
sections.content:
Each GSS-API mechanism has a SASL name that identifies it. A mechanism name without the suffix -PLUS indicates that the server does not support channel binding; adding that suffix identifies the channel-binding form.

When a mechanism has no registered friendly name, GS2 derives one from its object identifier. The RFC also assigns the friendly names GS2-KRB5 and GS2-KRB5-PLUS for the Kerberos V5 mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: A SASL mechanism name tells the client which GSS-API mechanism is available. The -PLUS ending marks the version that supports channel binding.

sections.title: The Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
The client always starts the GSS-API exchange. The SASL messages usually carry the GSS-API context tokens directly; the initial token also gets a GS2 header.

The header carries a channel-binding flag and may carry an authorization identity. It also indicates when the initial GSS-API token lacks the standard header that a server would otherwise restore before processing it.
sections.plainLanguage: The client begins authentication and sends the GSS-API tokens through SASL. A short first-message header tells the server how channel binding is being used and may identify the requested authorization identity.

sections.title: Negotiating Channel Binding
sections.content:
Channel binding connects authentication to an external secure channel, such as TLS, so an attacker cannot easily move an authentication exchange to a different connection. The client indicates whether it used a binding, does not support one, or supports one but believes the server does not.

The server must reject incompatible choices, such as a client requiring a binding the server does not support. When an application has no other binding agreement, tls-unique is the default channel-binding type specified by this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Channel binding ties the login exchange to the secure connection carrying it. The client and server must agree on the binding method or authentication fails.

sections.title: What GS2 Does Not Protect
sections.content:
GS2 provides no SASL security layers. It does not protect application messages sent after authentication, or plaintext exchanged outside the mechanism. Applications that need integrity or confidentiality must use a protected external channel or another SASL mechanism.

The security of a GS2 exchange depends on its GSS-API mechanism and, when used, the external channel and its binding data. The RFC prohibits GSS-API mechanisms that negotiate other mechanisms, including SPNEGO, from being used as GS2 mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: GS2 authenticates the peers but does not encrypt the application data that follows. Use a secure external channel or another mechanism when later messages also need protection.
